title: CHAPTER FIFTEEN. On the intellect of God; definition
english: CHAPTER FIFTEEN. On the intellect of God.

The intellect of God is His highest perfection, by which He distinctly, most inwardly, and most perfectly knows all and each things which in any way are, were, will be, or can be, and the order, connection, and various respects of all and each among themselves which they have and can have, and their opposites.

Intellect, so called by the Latins from inter and lego, by force of etymology notes the power, act, and habit by which we know so as to have choice between this and that — which is to know so as to discern. The material in this attribute also is the same as in the others, namely God's highest perfection. But the formal consists in the position of the most supereminent mode of spiritual life by which God most perfectly understands all things.

title: Proofs 1-5 that God has intellect
english: That this truly belongs to God we prove in this way. FIRST, from the clear testimonies of sacred Scripture: Genesis 6:5; Job 28:23; Psalm 94; Acts 1:24; 15:8, 18; 1 John 3:20; 1 Samuel 2:3 — Jehovah is the strong God endowed with all knowledge. SECOND, from the infinity of the divine nature. To whose essence is infinitely perfect, intellect belongs, and indeed infinite intellect.

THIRD, from spiritual life. Whoever lives spiritually also has intellect. But God lives spiritually — demonstrated in chapter XIV. FOURTH, from God's outward operations: whoever by the Word produces, preserves, bears, governs, and orders all things has intellect; and whoever grants intellect to others and illuminates it has intellect — Exodus 36; Psalm 16:7; 32:8; 119. FIFTH, from the consent of Gentile philosophers — Hermes Trismegistus, Iamblichus, Porphyry, Proclus, Anaxagoras, Aristotle, Zeno.

title: II-V: act, object, primary and secondary objects
english: II. But in the divine intellect there are to be distinctly considered act, object, order, mode, and use. III. The act is the comprehension of all knowables insofar as they are knowable — or, what amounts to the same, one perfect cognition. We say the act of the divine intellect according to itself and its substance with respect to all intelligibles is one and simple, seeing it is in reality God's very essence and intellect; yet from the varied termination of God's knowledge to diverse objects it is commonly conceived by us as manifold and receives diverse names — of wisdom, science, foreknowledge — which yet do not multiply the substance.

IV. The object of the intellect's act is every intelligible, or everything that can be known. Therefore God is called omniscient — Hebrews 4:13; 1 John 3:20. V. And it is primary, namely God Himself, or secondary, anything besides God. The divine essence is the primary object of the divine intellect by primacy of dignity, order, power, and adequation.

title: VI-VIII: threefold order of knowable objects
english: VI. The order of knowable objects is threefold. First, of those which are simply necessary, and which from eternity always were, and all possibles insofar as they are only possible — such is God Himself and whatever naturally is in God. VII. Second is of those which are not eternal and simply necessary, yet truly are existing each in its own mode, either by proper act or at least in their causes — heaven, earth, angels, humans; accidents; past, present, future.

VIII. Third is of those which are necessary neither simply nor from hypothesis, but either only possible, or even altogether impossible and contradictory — as David betrayed by the men of Keilah if he had remained (1 Samuel 23:11); the Tyrians and Sidonians if the Gospel had been preached (Matthew 11:21); that it is impossible for God to perish or lie. From which it is gathered that nothing at all escapes Him.

title: IX-X: mode of divine knowing; thirteen theorems
english: IX. The mode of knowing is to be estimated both from the condition of the knowable object and from the nature of God's intellect. For God understands no thing otherwise than as it itself stands, because He is the God of truth. But God knows in a divine mode — most perfectly, not through intelligible species, not by discursive reasoning, but by thoroughly penetrating all things with His intellect through His own essence alone, except evils which He knows through opposite goods.

X. That mode of knowing in the divine intellect is considered in genus or in species. In genus, these theorems explain it: (1) As is the nature of    knowables, so also is their science in God. (2) God first knows Himself. (3) He knows Himself wholly and adequately. (4) Other things besides Himself He knows wholly — excellently as in Himself, adequately as in their proper natures. (5) God's understanding is His being and essence. (6) God does not understand successively or by discourse, but by a simple and infinite intuition. (7) From eternity He knows all things, nothing newly. (8) He knows all things immensely. (9) He knows all things immutably. (10) By one individual act He knows all things. (11) God understands all things holily. (12) God's intellect depends on no external cause. (13) God's intellect is always certain and can never be deceived, not even in future contingents.

title: XI-XXI: distinctions of divine science
english: XI. But in species the schools distinguish God's science, which in itself is unique and most simple, according to various objects and respects to objects. XII. It is science of simple intelligence or of vision. In the first instant of reason they place science of simple intelligence; in the second, decrees of free will; in the third, science of vision. Some set a fourth instant after the first, in which they consider a middle science before free will's decrees.

XIII. Science of simple intelligence is the cognition of all possibles, preceding in God the free act of will. XIV. Science of vision is that by which God, after the decree of will, knows besides Himself all other things which are, will be, or have been. XV–XVII. It is natural or free — natural nearly the same as simple intelligence; free that by which God after the free act of His will distinctly understands all future things. XVIII–XX. It is theoretical or practical. XXI. These and like distinctions are taken from our mode of knowing. I do not deny the thing itself of middle science, but make it a part of simple intelligence; a science distinct from simple intelligence and vision does not seem needed.

title: XXII-XXIV: theoretical and practical uses — Cap. 15 COMPLETE
english: XXII. Still concerning mode: there follows a manifold use. The first is theoretical, both for confirmation of orthodox faith and for elenchus and refutation of various error. XXIII. For this doctrine confirms the catholic faith concerning God's omniscience; and it refutes those who confuse the distinct modes of divine science, who set absolute foreknowledge of things certainly future before the divine decree, make it the cause of things, and from the certainty of divine foreknowledge take away the contingency of things.

Things are not future because God knows them, but because they are future they are known by God — Origen, Chrysostom, Ambrose; Augustine speaks of active science joined with will and power. XXIV. The other use is practical: pedagogical, corrective, consolatory — that we may live holily in God's eyes (Psalm 139); that we may beware evils of fault; that the conscience of things well done may be consoled against unjust judgments, by the argument of Psalm 7; 1 Corinthians 4:5; 2 Corinthians 10:18.
